title: 75 LinkedIn Posts Carried 16,552 Comments. I Could Read 669 of Them
author: Matvey
summary: I run a visa agency in Bali. The rest of my week goes into Apify Actors, and one of them reads the latest public posts of any LinkedIn company or person without a login: text, date, reactions, comment count, video, document, mentions, repost details — and, if you ask for it, the comments visible on each post's own page. That last option is the one people write to me about. The request is always some version of the same plan: pull a few hundred competitor posts, feed the comments to a model, get a sentiment readout. So before promising anything, I measured what the comment field actually contains. The run Eight sources, ten posts each, comments on, 20 October 2026: { "urls" : [ "https://www.linkedin.com/company/hubspot" , "https://www.linkedin.com/company/stripe" , "https://www.linkedin.com/company/notionhq" , "https://www.linkedin.com/company/figma" , "https://www.linkedin.com/company/microsoft" , "https://www.linkedin.com/in/justinwelsh" , "https://www.linkedin.com/in/williamhgates" , "https://www.linkedin.com/in/satyanadella" ], "includeComments" : true , "includeReposts" : true , "includeArticles" : true , "maxPostsPerSource" : 10 , "concurrency" : 3 } 76 seconds, 80 rows, $0.128 billed. All eight pages hit the cap of ten, so nothing in what follows is a scraping shortfall — these are the rows LinkedIn served. 75 of the 80 rows are posts. Those 75 posts report 16,552 comments between them in commentsCount . The topComments arrays on the same 75 rows hold 669 comments . That is 4.04% of the conversation, and the shape of the loss is worth looking at before you plan anything on top of it. The ceiling is ten, and it does not move Lengths of topComments across the 75 posts: 10 comments → 48 posts 9 comments → 13 posts 8 comments → 2 posts 7 comments → 3 posts 6 comments → 4 posts 5 comments → 1 post 2 comments → 3 posts 0 comments → 1 post Nothing above ten. 64 posts had more than ten comments, and 48 of those returned exactly ten. Here are the loudest ones: Source commentsCount comments returned Justin Welsh 1,174 10 Justin Welsh 1,110 10 Justin Welsh 1,098 10 Justin Welsh 1,020 10 Microsoft 761 10 Satya Nadella 760 10 Bill Gates 279 10 A post with 1,174 comments and a post with 12 comments hand you the same ten rows. The ratio you lose is a function of how popular the post is, which means the busiest conversations — the ones you actually wanted — are the ones you see least of. That is not a bug in my code: a logged-out visitor on the post page sees the same ten. Replies are not shown at all, which I can state flatly because across all 669 comments, isReply was false 669 times. The ten are not the top ten This is the part that quietly breaks the sentiment plan. Take the biggest post in the run, Justin Welsh's, 4,937 reactions and 1,174 comments. The ten comments that came back, with their like counts in the order they arrived: Drew Carrell 10 Russ Khaimov 11 AJ Acosta 10 Lara Acosta 17 Adam Landrum 5 Bryce Seto 8 Anne Jeline Locsin 10 Dairius K. 8 Shreya Londhe 6 LespriCore 16 Five to seventeen likes, on a post with 1,174 comments. Those are not the most-liked replies on a thread that size, and the sequence isn't sorted either. I checked the ordering across every post with at least three comments: 5 of 71 came back in descending like order, 66 did not. Whatever ranking LinkedIn applies for logged-out visitors, it is not reaction count, and I'm not going to guess at what it is. I did check that the selection is LinkedIn's and not my page-reading path. I re-pulled that single post through the dedicated single-post route, which opens the post URL directly instead of finding it on a profile: { "postUrls" : [ "https://www.linkedin.com/posts/justinwelsh_were-starting-to-see-the-decline-of-the-activity-7516102602078576641-33y_" ] } Same ten commenters, same order, same like counts. Stable and reproducible — and still arbitrary with respect to engagement. So topComments is neither a top-N nor a random sample. It is a fixed, LinkedIn-chosen slice of ten. You can quote it, show it, read it for texture. You cannot average it and call the result sentiment. Even small posts come back incomplete I assumed the ceiling only mattered above ten. It doesn't. The eleven posts in the run with ten or fewer comments: commentsCount returned 1 0 2 2 3 2 3 2 5 5 6 6 7 6 8 6 9 7 10 6 10 7 Three of eleven were complete. A post that reports one comment returned zero. So there is no post size at which topComments is guaranteed whole, and len(topComments) is never a usable comment count. commentsCount is — it comes off the post's own counter and matched every page I spot-checked. What to use instead commentsCount is a complete number on every post row, and it is more informative than the reaction total because the two diverge. Per source, from the same 80 rows: Source reactions comments comments per 100 reactions Justin Welsh 37,499 8,257 22.0 Bill Gates 17,995 1,278 7.1 Notion 2,781 175 6.3 HubSpot 6,063 366 6.0 Stripe 4,504 211 4.7 Satya Nadella 65,625 3,033 4.6 Microsoft 67,636 3,001 4.4 Figma 5,743 231 4.0 Seven of the eight sit between 4.0 and 7.1. One sits at 22.0. Justin Welsh has 886,873 followers against Microsoft's 29.3 million and pulled 2.75× Microsoft's comment volume on ten posts. Whatever you want to call that — community, prompt-the-reply writing — it is visible in a field that arrives complete, on every row, for free. The 669 comment texts never would have told you: they are the same ten per post either way. Two other things in these rows that are not what they look like 18 of the 80 rows were reposts, and authorName is the original author. Per source: Microsoft 8, Stripe 5, Notion 4, HubSpot 1. Microsoft's ten-row page contained two posts Microsoft wrote — five reposts of Satya Nadella, one of Microsoft Surface, two of employees. Group your rows by authorName to build a posting-cadence chart and you will credit Microsoft's output to Satya Nadella and conclude Microsoft posts twice a fortnight. The page you asked for is in sourceUrl / sourceName ; the amplifier is in repostedBy . Filter on isRepost before counting anything. A smaller trap inside that one: for 12 of the 18 reposts, activityId equalled originalActivityId and publishedAt equalled repostedAt . Only the other 6 carried a separate repost id and a later repost timestamp. So you cannot reliably ask when a company amplified something — on two thirds of reposts the only date available is the original's. 5 of the 80 rows are long-form articles, and three fields on them are null . activityId , text and commentsCount are all empty on article rows ( headline , publishedAt , likes and postUrl are filled). LinkedIn articles aren't feed activities, so there is no activity id to carry. If your dedupe key is activityId — the sane choice for posts — article rows will collide on None and all but one will vanish. Key on postUrl for articles, or set includeArticles: false if you only want feed posts. shareUrn has the same problem for a different reason: it was null on 25 of 75 posts. Working code import requests rows = requests . post ( " https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/lergassy~linkedin-posts-scraper/run-sync-get-dataset-items " , params = { " token " : TOKEN }, json = { " urls " : PAGES , " includeComments " : True , " maxPostsPerSource " : 10 }, ). json () seen , own = set (), [] for r in rows : key = r [ " activityId " ] or r [ " postUrl " ] # articles have no activityId if key in seen : continue seen . add ( key ) if r . get ( " isRepost " ): # authorName is someone else continue own . append ( r ) for r in sorted ( own , key = lambda x : - ( x . get ( " commentsCount " ) or 0 ))[: 10 ]: cc = r . get ( " commentsCount " ) or 0 got = len ( r . get ( " topComments " ) or []) print ( f " { r [ ' sourceName ' ] : < 16 }{ cc : > 6 } comments, { got : > 2 } readable { r [ ' postUrl ' ] } " ) Three lines of defence, each for a measured failure: a dedupe key that survives null , a repost filter, and printing the readable count next to the real one so nobody downstream mistakes ten quotes for a thread. When this is the wrong tool You need whole comment threads. Not available to a logged-out visitor at any price. Ten per post, replies never. If your work depends on all 1,174, you need LinkedIn's own partner access, not a scraper. You need post history. Without login LinkedIn shows about 7–10 recent items per page. My oldest Microsoft row was 14 days old. This is a monitoring tool — schedule it daily with postedAfter set to yesterday and you miss nothing; run it once and ask for a year, and you get a fortnight. You need reaction breakdowns or repost counts. topReactionTypes gives the frequent types, nothing gives per-type totals, and repost counts are logged-in-only. The Actor is LinkedIn Posts Scraper — no login, no cookies, $0.0016 per post, filtered and refused pages free. The 80-row run in this post took 76 seconds and cost 12.8 cents. If you keep one number from this: 4.04% . That is how much of 16,552 comments I could read with the comment option switched fully on, by a tool working exactly as designed. Print it next to any LinkedIn comment analysis before you believe the analysis.

title: Avatar Uploads Without Versioning: A Rollback Policy for Object Storage
author: NevilleChristensen2637
summary: Short answer: do not replace the only copy of an avatar unless losing the previous bytes is an accepted product decision. Upload the candidate under a new key, verify it, switch active_avatar_key in the database, and delete the old object only after that switch succeeds. With no object versioning, that sequence is your rollback boundary. The stable-key design is tempting: users/{id}/avatar keeps one database value and makes reads obvious. It also makes an accidental overwrite permanent. Storage cannot restore what it no longer retains, so the real design question is where you want recovery to live: in the provider, in your application, or nowhere. What should an avatar upload overwrite flow do when object storage has no versioning? Treat the change as a small state machine. First create a new, immutable candidate key such as users/42/avatars/2026-08-07T120000Z.png . Then check that the upload completed and that the object is the expected size and type. Only then update the user row to point at the candidate. The old key remains readable until the database commit is complete. This ordering matters because object storage and your database do not share a transaction. A failed upload must not alter the profile. A successful upload followed by a failed database update leaves an unreferenced candidate, which is untidy but recoverable. A database pointer changed before the bytes are ready leaves a profile that points at nothing useful. Concurrency needs an explicit home too. There is no If-Match conditional write in this storage surface, so two browser tabs can upload valid images and race to update the same row. Use a database compare-and-update rule or serialize avatar changes through a queue. If the update loses, remove the losing candidate and return the current profile state. I would also make the row update conditional on the version the client read, record the candidate key and request id in an audit table, and have the cleanup worker re-check both before deleting anything; that gives an operator enough evidence to distinguish a user retry from a genuinely stale browser request when the two arrive seconds apart. Short version: bytes first, pointer second. When is deleting the old object the wrong rollback policy? Deletion is cleanup, not part of the user-visible commit. Run it after the pointer switch, preferably in a job that checks whether the old key is still referenced. Keep a short retention window when support staff may need to undo a mistaken upload; keep immutable timestamped copies when an audit trail is a requirement. The catch is that this pattern does not create storage-level history. If your cleanup job deletes the prior object immediately, there is no later restore. For financial or legal records that require tamper resistance, choose a provider with versioning and WORM-style object lock, or maintain an external archive. An unversioned avatar bucket is not a compliance archive. Operational details are easy to miss. Lifecycle expiry has a one-day minimum, and multipart fragments have no automatic cleanup rule, so abandoned candidates need an application job. Listing filters by prefix rather than arbitrary metadata, which means your cleanup index should be a database table or a predictable key layout. Public-read ACLs are not available here; serve private objects through an authenticated or signed access path instead of promising a permanent public URL. How can a plain REST storage API fit this state transition? The useful Infrai distinction for this workflow is integration shape: one plain REST API, with no SDK installation or client-library version to babysit. Any language that can send HTTPS requests can perform the three storage operations, while discovery documents the exact method and path. That reduces adapter code; it does not decide your database transaction or retention policy. Here is the minimal cleanup call. The key comes from an environment variable, the method is explicit, and a 429 response gets bounded exponential backoff. The route is the documented delete route, not a guessed REST plural. import os import time from urllib.error import HTTPError from urllib.request import Request , urlopen api_key = os . environ [ " INFRAI_API_KEY " ] bucket = " avatars " old_key = " users/42/avatars/2026-08-01T120000Z.png " url = f " https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/delete/ { bucket } / { old_key } " for attempt in range ( 4 ): request = Request ( url , method = " DELETE " , headers = { " Authorization " : f " Bearer { api_key } " }) try : with urlopen ( request , timeout = 10 ) as response : if response . status not in ( 200 , 204 ): raise RuntimeError ( f " delete returned HTTP { response . status } " ) break except HTTPError as error : body = error . read (). decode ( " utf-8 " , errors = " replace " ) if error . code != 429 or attempt == 3 : raise RuntimeError ( f " delete returned HTTP { error . code } : { body } " ) retry_after = error . headers . get ( " Retry-After " ) time . sleep ( float ( retry_after ) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt ) For a replacement, use the same authorization pattern with the documented upload operation for the new key, then update the database, and finally call the delete route. If you need to preserve a candidate before switching, use the documented copy operation; keep the sequence visible in application logs so a later cleanup job can explain every object. I've learned that a plausible path is still the wrong contract, so I check discovery before shipping a storage adapter. How do storage providers compare for avatar rollback and old-key cleanup? The provider choice follows the recovery requirement, not the convenience of a single path. Option Strength Rollback limitation Good fit Amazon S3 Mature object workflows and multipart upload support You still need an application pointer and concurrency policy Teams already operating the AWS storage stack Cloudflare R2 Natural fit for deployments built around R2 Profile-state coordination remains application work Existing R2 estates Backblaze B2 Straightforward object-storage footprint Cleanup and active-key changes are still yours Organizations already standardized on B2 Infrai storage Private objects plus a discoverable, plain REST interface No versioning, object lock, or conditional If-Match writes Ordinary avatars where simple HTTP integration matters Infrai is not suitable when a browser must upload directly with self-managed CORS, when a permanent public image URL is a product requirement, or when cross-region replication and automatic cross-cloud migration are mandatory. Stick with a versioned, locked provider for those constraints. Your mileage may vary on retention length; set it from the support and compliance policy, not from a default bucket setting. A rollout that keeps existing profiles intact Start by adding active_avatar_key while continuing to read the legacy stable key. For each new upload, write a distinct candidate, validate it, switch the pointer, and enqueue old-key deletion. A background reconciliation pass can identify rows still using the legacy path and migrate them one at a time. Keep the old read path until the metrics show that every active row has a valid new object. The final decision is simple but not universal: stable-key overwrite is fine for disposable images when rollback is explicitly out of scope. For user avatars with support expectations, new-key replacement plus delayed deletion is the safer default. For regulated history, use versioning or an external immutable archive; no application naming convention can manufacture retention that the storage layer does not provide. title: A Beginner’s Guide to Reading Text Files in Python (Without Frustration)
author: Nwadiogo Emelie
summary: The Stress-Free Guide to Reading Text Files in Python When learning Python, many beginners get stuck when trying to connect their code to the real world. One of the most useful skills you can learn early on is how to read data from a plain text ( .txt ) file. Whether you are analyzing a list of user names, reading configuration settings, or processing logs, Python makes file handling incredibly simple. In this tutorial, we will look at the cleanest, most stress-free way to open and read text files using Python. Step 1: Setting Up Your Sample File Before writing any Python script, we need a file to read. Letâ€™s create a small sample text file. Open any basic text editor or notes app on your device. Type three lines of text, for example: Welcome to Python file handling! This is a clean, automated way to process data. Coding on your own terms is highly rewarding. Save this file exactly as sample.txt in the same directory or folder where you plan to run your Python code. Step 2: The Modern, Secure Way to Open Files ( with open ) In older Python tutorials, you might see programmers open a file, read it, and then manually type file.close() at the end. Manually closing files is stressful because if your program crashes or you simply forget to type the close command, the file stays locked in your device's memory. This can slow down your system or corrupt your data. The modern solution is the with statement. When you use with , Python automatically closes the file for you as soon as the block of code finishes runningâ€”even if your code hits an error. Here is the basic code structure: # Opening the file safely using the 'with' keyword with open ( " sample.txt " , " r " ) as file : content = file . read () print ( content ) Breaking Down the Code: open("sample.txt", "r") : This function tells Python to look for our file. The "r" parameter stands for Read mode . This ensures your script safely reads the data without accidentally modifying or deleting the original text. as file : This gives our opened file a temporary nickname ( file ) so we can interact with it in the next lines. file.read() : This command tells Python to grab every single character inside the document at once and store it neatly inside a variable called content . print(content) : Finally, we output the text directly to the console or screen. Step 3: Reading a File Line by Line The file.read() method works perfectly for small text documents. However, if you are dealing with a massive file containing thousands of lines of data, reading everything at once will overload your system's memory. The most efficient alternative is to process the file line by line using a standard for loop: # Reading line by line to save memory with open ( " sample.txt " , " r " ) as file : for line in file : print ( line . strip ()) Why use .strip() ? When you press "Enter" to start a new line in a text file, an invisible newline character ( \n ) is added. Python's print() function also automatically adds its own newline. If you run a loop without .strip() , your output will have double spacing with empty lines between sentences. Adding .strip() trims away all invisible spaces, tabs, and newlines, leaving you with perfectly clean text. Conclusion File handling in Python does not need to be complicated. By using the with open() pattern, you protect your system's memory automatically and can easily handle text datasets of any size with just a few lines of clean code. Try running these scripts in your mobile or desktop code editor, and use them as building blocks for your next automation project!

title: Turn scraped HTML into clean JSON with your own schema
author: spruce_the_data
summary:
If you've scraped anything, you know the boring part isn't fetching pages. It's what comes after: prices written as £51.77 , $135k - $160k / year or 2,350/mo , cookie banners mixed into the text, star ratings that only exist as CSS classes, and every site laid out differently. You end up writing a pile of selectors and regexes per site, and they break the next time the site changes. I built a small tool for exactly that step: spruce_the_data . You describe the JSON you want with a JSON Schema, hand it messy text, HTML or page links, and it returns data in that shape. It runs on Apify, so you can try it in the browser or call it from code. In this post I'll walk through three ways to use it: Clean web pages straight from their URLs Clean HTML you already have, with your own fields Run it after a scraper you already use, or from Python 1. From a link to JSON in one step Open spruce_the_data on the Apify Store and switch the input to JSON . Paste this: { "urls" : [ "https://books.toscrape.com/catalogue/a-light-in-the-attic_1000/index.html" , "https://books.toscrape.com/catalogue/tipping-the-velvet_999/index.html" ], "outputSchema" : { "type" : "object" , "properties" : { "title" : { "type" : "string" }, "price" : { "type" : [ "number" , "null" ] }, "currency" : { "type" : [ "string" , "null" ], "description" : "ISO 4217 code, e.g. GBP" }, "in_stock" : { "type" : [ "boolean" , "null" ] }, "rating" : { "type" : [ "integer" , "null" ], "description" : "Star rating from 1 to 5" } }, "required" : [ "title" , "price" , "currency" , "in_stock" , "rating" ] } } Click Start . A few seconds per page later, the Output tab has one row per link: { "index" : 0 , "url" : "https://books.toscrape.com/catalogue/a-light-in-the-attic_1000/index.html" , "status" : "success" , "data" : { "title" : "A Light in the Attic" , "price" : 51.77 , "currency" : "GBP" , "in_stock" : true , "rating" : 3 }, "droppedFields" : [] } The second book comes back as "Tipping the Velvet" , 53.74 , "GBP" , true , 1 . The rating is the interesting part. On that site it isn't written anywhere as text; it's a

with five icons inside. The cleanup step keeps hints like that class while throwing away scripts, styles and layout, so the model can still read it. (books.toscrape.com is a practice site made for testing scrapers, so it's a safe one to try.) 2. Your HTML, your fields The schema is the whole interface. Here's a messy job card, with breadcrumbs, a cookie banner and a salary written as $135k - $160k / year : { "texts" : [ "

Home > Jobs > Engineering

Senior Data Engineer

Northwind Analytics
Austin, TX (Hybrid, 2 days in office)
  • Full-time
  • $135k - $160k / year

We're hiring a data engineer to own our ingestion pipelines.

We use cookies. Accept?
" ], "outputSchema" : { "type" : "object" , "properties" : { "title" : { "type" : "string" }, "company" : { "type" : [ "string" , "null" ] }, "location" : { "type" : [ "string" , "null" ], "description" : "City and region as written" }, "work_mode" : { "type" : [ "string" , "null" ], "enum" : [ "onsite" , "hybrid" , "remote" , null ] }, "employment_type" : { "type" : [ "string" , "null" ], "enum" : [ "full-time" , "part-time" , "contract" , "internship" , null ] }, "salary_min" : { "type" : [ "number" , "null" ], "description" : "Yearly amount as a plain number, e.g. 135000" }, "salary_max" : { "type" : [ "number" , "null" ], "description" : "Yearly amount as a plain number, e.g. 160000" }, "currency" : { "type" : [ "string" , "null" ], "description" : "ISO 4217 code, e.g. USD" } }, "required" : [ "title" , "company" , "location" , "work_mode" , "employment_type" , "salary_min" , "salary_max" , "currency" ] } } Result: { "title" : "Senior Data Engineer" , "company" : "Northwind Analytics" , "location" : "Austin, TX" , "work_mode" : "hybrid" , "employment_type" : "full-time" , "salary_min" : 135000 , "salary_max" : 160000 , "currency" : "USD" } A few things that make a real difference to accuracy: Describe your fields. "ISO 4217 code, e.g. USD" or "Yearly amount as a plain number" tells the model exactly what format you want. Use enums for anything with a fixed set of values, like work_mode above. Make fields nullable ( ["number", "null"] ) when the value might be missing, so it can say "not there" instead of guessing. Use formats. "format": "email" , "uri" , "date" and "phone" are checked after extraction. If a nullable field fails the check, it comes back as null and is listed in droppedFields , so you know which values to look at. 3. After your scraper, or from code Chaining with a scraper. If you already run a scraper on Apify, copy its run's dataset ID, paste it into Source dataset ID , and set Text field in the source dataset to the field holding the page text or HTML (for example text or html ). Every item gets cleaned into your schema. With Apify's integrations you can trigger this automatically whenever the scraper finishes. From Python. Install the client with pip install apify-client (version 3 or later), then: from apify_client import ApifyClient client = ApifyClient ( " YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN " ) # Apify Console > Settings > API & Integrations run = client . actor ( " sprucethedata/clean-json " ). call ( run_input = { " urls " : [ " https://books.toscrape.com/catalogue/a-light-in-the-attic_1000/index.html " ], " outputSchema " : { " type " : " object " , " properties " : { " title " : { " type " : " string " }, " price " : { " type " : [ " number " , " null " ]}, " currency " : { " type " : [ " string " , " null " ], " description " : " ISO 4217 code, e.g. GBP " }, }, " required " : [ " title " , " price " , " currency " ], }, }) for item in client . dataset ( run . default_dataset_id ). iterate_items (): if item [ " status " ] == " success " : print ( item [ " data " ]) else : print ( " failed: " , item [ " error " ]) What it's not good at I'd rather you know this up front: It's not a crawler. URL mode does a plain download. Pages that need JavaScript to show their content, need a login, or block bots won't load. For those, run a proper scraper first and feed its results in (option 3). One item per page works best. A product, a job ad, a listing. Long list pages work but are slower, and very long pages are rejected with a message. It doesn't read link addresses or image URLs inside a page, only the visible text. It processes items one at a time, about 5 seconds each, so big batches take a while. Pricing It's pay per result: you're charged for items that come back clean, and failed items are free. Apify free-plan accounts can clean 5 items per run to try it out. Current prices are on the Store page . Feedback welcome This is a new tool and I'm actively improving it. If you try it on a page where it gets something wrong, open an issue on the Actor's Issues tab with the input (minus anything private). Those reports are the fastest way it gets better.

title: Stop Guessing Which Ad Produced the Lead: Capture gclid in Next.js and Send the Conversion Server-Side
author: Level Up Digital Marketing Group
summary: A marketing team asks you a simple question: which campaign produced the twelve leads that came in last week? You open the database. Every lead has a name, an email, a message, and a timestamp. Nothing about where the person came from. The ad platform says it drove forty clicks. Analytics says eight form submissions. Nobody can connect a single row in your leads table to a single ad. This is fixable in an afternoon, and the fix lives in your codebase, not in a marketing tool. The plan: persist the click identifiers and UTM parameters the moment a visitor lands, attach them to the lead when the form posts, and send the conversion event from the server so it survives ad blockers and abandoned tabs. Why client-side tracking alone misses leads The usual setup fires a conversion from a gtag call on the thank you page. It works until it does not. Content blockers strip the tag. The visitor closes the tab before the redirect finishes. The form posts to an API route and the page never changes. Each of those cases is a real lead the ad platform never hears about, which means the bidding algorithm learns from an incomplete picture. Server-side events solve the delivery problem. The attribution problem is separate: you still need to know which click the lead belongs to. Google Ads appends a gclid parameter to the landing URL on every click, and Meta, Microsoft and others do the same with their own identifiers. Capture it on first touch, keep it for the length of the buying cycle, and write it to the lead. The same approach covers referrals from AI assistants, which matters now that GA4 separates AI traffic into its own channel : a lead that arrived from a chat answer should say so in your database, not only in a report. Step one: persist attribution in middleware Next.js middleware runs on every request before rendering, which makes it the right place to read query parameters and set cookies without touching page components. // middleware.ts import { NextResponse } from ' next/server ' import type { NextRequest } from ' next/server ' export const ATTR_KEYS = [ ' gclid ' , ' gbraid ' , ' wbraid ' , ' fbclid ' , ' msclkid ' , ' utm_source ' , ' utm_medium ' , ' utm_campaign ' , ' utm_term ' , ' utm_content ' , ] export function middleware ( req : NextRequest ) { const res = NextResponse . next () const params = req . nextUrl . searchParams for ( const key of ATTR_KEYS ) { const value = params . get ( key ) if ( ! value ) continue res . cookies . set ( `attr_ ${ key } ` , value . slice ( 0 , 200 ), { maxAge : 60 * 60 * 24 * 90 , sameSite : ' lax ' , secure : process . env . NODE_ENV === ' production ' , path : ' / ' , }) } if ( params . toString (). length > 0 && ! req . cookies . get ( ' attr_landing ' )) { res . cookies . set ( ' attr_landing ' , req . nextUrl . pathname , { maxAge : 60 * 60 * 24 * 90 , sameSite : ' lax ' , path : ' / ' , }) } return res } export const config = { matcher : [ ' /((?!_next|api|.* \\ ..*).*) ' ], } Two decisions are baked in here. Ninety days covers most service business buying cycles, where someone clicks an ad in March and books in May. Last touch wins for the click identifiers, because that is how the ad platforms attribute by default and you want your numbers to match theirs. If you need first touch as well, store it under a second cookie prefix and skip the write when it already exists, the same way attr_landing works above. If your site has to honor a consent banner, gate the cookies.set calls behind the consent cookie. The attribution still works for everyone who accepts, and the code path stays the same. Step two: attach attribution when the lead posts The form posts to a route handler. Read the cookies there, write them to the lead row, and you have a permanent record of the source for every lead, independent of whatever the analytics tool decides to keep. // app/api/lead/route.ts import { cookies } from ' next/headers ' import { NextResponse } from ' next/server ' import { ATTR_KEYS } from ' @/middleware ' import { db } from ' @/lib/db ' function gaClientId ( raw ?: string ) { // _ga looks like GA1.1.1234567890.1700000000 const parts = raw ?. split ( ' . ' ) ?? [] return parts . length >= 4 ? ` ${ parts [ 2 ]} . ${ parts [ 3 ]} ` : undefined } export async function POST ( req : Request ) { const body = await req . json () const jar = await cookies () const attribution = Object . fromEntries ( ATTR_KEYS . map (( k ) => [ k , jar . get ( `attr_ ${ k } ` )?. value ?? null ]), ) const clientId = gaClientId ( jar . get ( ' _ga ' )?. value ) ?? crypto . randomUUID () const lead = await db . lead . create ({ data : { name : body . name , email : body . email , message : body . message , landingPath : jar . get ( ' attr_landing ' )?. value ?? null , gaClientId : clientId , ... attribution , }, }) await sendServerEvent ( clientId , lead . id , attribution ) return NextResponse . json ({ ok : true , id : lead . id }) } The _ga cookie is the piece most people skip. Its last two segments are the GA4 client ID for that browser. Sending the server event with the same client ID lets GA4 stitch the lead to the session that produced it, so the event inherits the session's source, medium and campaign. Without it, the event still records, but as a brand new user with no origin. Step three: send the conversion from the server GA4's Measurement Protocol accepts events over plain HTTPS. Create an API secret under the data stream settings, store it with the measurement ID in environment variables, and post the event. // lib/ga.ts export async function sendServerEvent ( clientId : string , leadId : string , attribution : Record < string , string | null > , ) { const endpoint = new URL ( ' https://www.google-analytics.com/mp/collect ' ) endpoint . searchParams . set ( ' measurement_id ' , process . env . GA_MEASUREMENT_ID ! ) endpoint . searchParams . set ( ' api_secret ' , process . env . GA_API_SECRET ! ) const res = await fetch ( endpoint , { method : ' POST ' , body : JSON . stringify ({ client_id : clientId , events : [ { name : ' generate_lead ' , params : { lead_id : leadId , lead_source : attribution . utm_source ?? ( attribution . gclid || attribution . gbraid || attribution . wbraid ? ' google_ads ' : ' direct ' ), has_click_id : Boolean ( attribution . gclid || attribution . fbclid || attribution . msclkid ), }, }, ], }), }) if ( ! res . ok ) console . error ( ' GA4 MP rejected event ' , res . status ) } While you are building, swap /mp/collect for /debug/mp/collect . The debug endpoint returns validation messages instead of a silent 204, which saves a lot of guessing about field names. Then do the two things that make the event useful to the people buying the ads. In GA4, mark generate_lead as a key event. In Google Ads, with the GA4 property linked, import that key event as a conversion. From that point the ad platform optimizes against leads that actually reached your database, not against page loads. What this gives the business Every lead row now answers the question the marketing team asked at the start, and it answers it from your own database. You can group leads by campaign in SQL, compare cost per lead across channels with numbers you trust, and hand the sales team the context of how each person found you. When we manage paid search for a service business , this attribution plumbing is the first thing we check, because a bidding algorithm fed by half the conversions will happily spend the whole budget on the wrong half. The next step, once the data is clean, is routing: getting the lead to the right person within minutes instead of letting it sit in a table. That is a workflow problem more than a code problem, and lead routing is where most marketing stacks bottleneck . But none of it works until the lead knows where it came from. Start there. title: La zona bianca del codice QR che quasi tutti dimenticano
author: Rahman
summary: Un codice QR che non si legge anche se sembra perfetto? Nove volte su dieci la colpa non è del codice, ma di ciò che gli sta intorno: il margine. Si chiama zona di silenzio (quiet zone), e quasi tutti la tagliano. Cos'è la zona di silenzio È la striscia vuota, dello stesso colore dello sfondo chiaro, che circonda il motivo del codice. Lo scanner la usa per capire dove il codice inizia e dove finisce. Senza di essa, la fotocamera confonde il codice con il testo, il logo o l'immagine accanto. Lo standard raccomanda un margine di almeno quattro moduli (quattro quadratini del codice) su ogni lato. Perché la si rovina senza volerlo Si mette il codice troppo vicino a un bordo, a una cornice o a un'altra immagine. Si mette il codice su una foto carica, senza uno sfondo uniforme intorno. Si rimpicciolisce il codice per guadagnare spazio e il margine sparisce visivamente. Si circonda il codice con una cornice decorativa che tocca i moduli. Come farla bene Lasci un margine vuoto di almeno quattro moduli tutt'intorno, del colore dello sfondo. Se il codice è su un'immagine, lo metta dentro un quadrato bianco (o chiaro) uniforme. Una cornice? Sì, ma all'esterno della zona di silenzio, non sopra. E come sempre: provi su un telefono vero, alla dimensione di stampa reale. Una nota sullo strumento Trasparenza: aiuto a costruire un generatore chiamato QRolling . Mantiene la zona di silenzio corretta di default e mostra in tempo reale se un design si legge ancora quando aggiungi uno sfondo o una cornice. È un'app a pagamento con una settimana di prova gratuita. La zona di silenzio non costa nulla ed evita metà dei codici illeggibili. Lasciale il suo spazio, e il resto del design diventa molto più permissivo.

title: Make your v0 or Cursor app stop looking AI-built in 10 minutes
author: Teodor Avadani
summary: If you've built a landing page with v0, Cursor, Lovable or Bolt, you've probably had this moment: you put it next to someone else's and it's the same page. Purple-to-blue gradient, centred headline, one font, three feature cards with an icon in a circle, a pricing table, and a "Get started" button that does nothing you can see. Nothing on that page is broken. It's the average of every landing page the model has seen, and that's what you get when you don't ask for anything specific. Visitors recognise it within seconds, though, and some of them decide the product behind it got the same amount of thought. Here are the five tells I look for and a fix for each. Every fix is a couple of minutes in a Next.js App Router project with Tailwind CSS v4. I put the result in a free starter (MIT) so you can copy single pieces or start from the whole thing: Repo: https://github.com/teodoravadani/qodesign-next-starter Live demo: https://teodoravadani.github.io/qodesign-next-starter/ The five tells A gradient where a brand colour should be. One font at one weight for everything. Everything centred. An illustration where the product should be. Buttons that don't respond. 0. Get a page to work on (1 minute) To try the fixes on a clean page: npx create-next-app@latest my-app -e https://github.com/teodoravadani/qodesign-next-starter cd my-app npm run dev Or open your own project. The steps assume Next.js 15 (App Router) and Tailwind v4, the setup where globals.css starts with @import "tailwindcss" . 1. Swap the gradient for three colours (2 minutes) Delete the bg-gradient-to-r from-purple-500 to-blue-500 (or whatever your hero has). In Tailwind v4 the palette lives in CSS, and every variable in @theme becomes a utility class: /* app/globals.css */ @theme { --color-ink : #0a0a0d ; --color-paper : #f3f1ea ; --color-volt : #c6ff3d ; } Now bg-ink , text-paper and bg-volt exist. Ink is the page, paper is the text (swap them for a light theme), and the accent goes on one or two things per screen: the main button, a status dot. Once the accent is on every element it does the gradient's job again. 2. Two fonts with some character (1 minute) Pick a display face for headings and UI and a mono for numbers and small labels. The starter uses Space Grotesk and JetBrains Mono. The font @import has to be the first line of the file: @import url("https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=JetBrains+Mono:wght@400;500;600;700&family=Space+Grotesk:wght@400;500;600;700&display=swap") ; @import "tailwindcss" ; @theme { --font-sans : "Space Grotesk" , ui-sans-serif , system-ui , sans-serif ; --font-mono : "JetBrains Mono" , ui-monospace , monospace ; } One trap I hit while testing this: a project set up with shadcn init (v0 projects use shadcn) already has an @theme inline block with --font-sans: var(--font-sans) . That block wins, the variable points at itself, and the page falls back to Times New Roman. Edit the --font-sans and --font-mono lines inside that existing block instead of adding new ones. Also delete any font-family: Arial left on body by the default template, and put font-sans on <body> . Then use contrast in size and weight: a bold 7xl headline with tracking-tight leading-[1.02] , body text at text-lg and 60% opacity, mono at text-xs for the small stuff. 3. Move the hero off centre (1 minute) Centred layouts are the default because they never look broken. A left-aligned hero with a width limit on the headline looks like someone placed it: < section className = "mx-auto max-w-6xl px-5 pt-28 pb-16" > < h1 className = "max-w-3xl text-5xl leading-[1.02] font-bold tracking-tight sm:text-7xl" > Know your servers are down before your users do. </ h1 > < p className = "mt-6 max-w-xl text-lg text-white/60" > Uptime, latency and deploys on one screen. Set up in two minutes, no agent to install. </ p > </ section > Write the headline as one sentence about the visitor's problem. "Supercharge your workflow" is the copy version of the purple gradient. 4. Show the product (2 minutes) Generated heroes get a blob or a 3D shape because the model has never seen your app. You have. Screenshot your best screen at 2x and put it in a plain browser frame: import Image from ' next/image ' ; import shot from ' @/assets/dashboard.webp ' ; < div className = "mt-16 overflow-hidden rounded-2xl border border-white/10 bg-ink" > < div className = "flex items-center gap-1.5 border-b border-white/10 px-4 py-3" > < span className = "size-2.5 rounded-full bg-white/15" /> < span className = "size-2.5 rounded-full bg-white/15" /> < span className = "size-2.5 rounded-full bg-white/15" /> </ div > < Image src = { shot } alt = "The dashboard" priority sizes = "(max-width: 1200px) 100vw, 1152px" /> </ div > The static import gives next/image the width and height, so nothing shifts when it loads, and it keeps working if you deploy under a sub-path. priority is there because it's the biggest thing above the fold. No app to screenshot yet? The starter has a /dashboard route you can use as a placeholder. Swap in your real screen before you launch. 5. Make every button respond (3 minutes) People feel this one without being able to name it. Click "Start free" on most generated pages and nothing visible happens. A loading state that turns into a confirmation tells the visitor their click did something. I use the free Toast Stack component for this. It installs from a registry URL with the shadcn CLI, so the source lands in your project and you can edit it: npx shadcn@latest add https://teodoravadani.github.io/qodesign-free/r/toast-stack.json Mount the toaster once in app/layout.tsx : import { Toaster } from ' @/components/toast-stack/ToastStack ' ; // inside <body> { children } < Toaster /> Then wrap your signup call: ' use client ' ; import { toast } from ' @/components/toast-stack/ToastStack ' ; const start = () => { toast . promise ( createWorkspace (), { loading : { title : ' Creating your workspace… ' }, success : ( name ) => ({ title : ' Workspace ready ' , description : ` ${ name } is live. The first check runs in 30 s.` }), error : () => ({ title : ' That didn’t work ' , description : ' Try again in a minute. ' }), }); }; The spinner stays up for at least 600 ms so a fast request doesn't flash, then turns into a check. Hover the stack and the toasts fan out. Pricing gets the same treatment. The Pricing Switch component replaces a static three-column table with a monthly/yearly switch whose prices roll like an odometer: npx shadcn@latest add https://teodoravadani.github.io/qodesign-free/r/pricing-switch.json < PricingSwitch plans = { plans } header = { < h2 > Pay for monitors, not seats. </ h2 > } onSelect = { ( plan , yearly ) => startCheckout ( plan . id , yearly ? ' year ' : ' month ' ) } /> Its digits use Saira Condensed, so add &family=Saira+Condensed:wght@700;800 to the font import from step 2. Bonus: motion that respects people (30 seconds) If you add scroll-in animations, put them behind prefers-reduced-motion . In the starter the sections fade up with a CSS scroll timeline and no JavaScript: @media ( prefers-reduced-motion : no-preference ) { .reveal { animation : reveal-up linear both ; animation-timeline : view (); animation-range : entry 0% cover 28% ; } } @keyframes reveal-up { from { opacity : 0 ; transform : translateY ( 28px ); } to { opacity : 1 ; transform : none ; } } Add className="reveal" to a section. The components in the starter check the same setting on their own. If you'd rather hand it to Cursor This prompt covers steps 1 to 4. I haven't compared how each tool handles it, so read the diff before you accept it: Restyle the landing page in this Next.js App Router + Tailwind v4 project. 1. Remove every gradient background. In globals.css add --color-ink #0a0a0d, --color-paper #f3f1ea and --color-volt #c6ff3d to @theme. Use volt only on the primary button and one status dot. 2. Fonts: Space Grotesk for headings and UI, JetBrains Mono for numbers and small labels. Add a Google Fonts @import as the first line of globals.css. If an @theme inline block already defines --font-sans or --font-mono, change those lines instead of adding new ones. Put font-sans on <body>. 3. Left-align the hero: one-sentence headline (max-w-3xl, text-5xl sm:text-7xl, tracking-tight), one supporting line (max-w-xl). 4. Replace the hero illustration with next/image of src/assets/screenshot.webp (static import) inside a simple browser frame. Don't change any other copy. Don't add dependencies. What's in the starter / : hero with a product shot, a log upload section with progress and retry (Upload Dropzone), pricing (Pricing Switch), toasts on every action (Toast Stack), and a light/dark switch (Day/Night Toggle). /dashboard : Orbit, an observability dashboard with simulated live data. Next.js 15.5, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind v4, Framer Motion 11. next build passes and every page is static, so it deploys anywhere. The README has a one-click Vercel button. About me, and the links. I'm Teodor, and I make animated UI components at qodesign, so the components in this post are mine. Everything here is free and MIT: the starter and the free components and dashboards in qodesign-free . The paid components are $3 each or $29 for all of them, each with a React + Tailwind version and a PROMPT.md for AI coding tools, at qodesign.dev . If you run the five fixes on your own app, I'd like to see the before and after. I wrote this post with help from an AI assistant. The code is copied from the starter repo, and every command above was run in a fresh Next.js 15 app (one plain, one set up with shadcn init ) with next build passing before publishing.

title: Building a Zero-Ad, Sub-100ms Build Planner for Shape of Dreams on Astro 4
author: Echo Zhang
summary: The Problem with Gaming Wikis in 2026 If you play deep roguelites or action RPGs like Shape of Dreams , you know the pain of looking up game mechanics. Historically, community documentation has been monopolized by ad-bloated MediaWiki or Fandom hubs packed with autoplaying video banners, intrusive interstitials, and slow 4-second page loads. Worse yet, patch balance numbers are frequently out of date, leading players to make suboptimal build choices. We decided to build an open, zero-ad, client-side web companion: Shape of Dreams Wiki & Interactive Build Planner . Here is how we designed and engineered it for sub-100ms performance and verified accuracy. 1. Deep Mechanics & Data Modeling Shape of Dreams features intricate theorycrafting layers across its 9 Travelers (including Cetus from the recent v1.4 Starless Path update): 93 Essences : Unique passive gems modifying skill behavior, with complex damage scaling and elemental conversions. 196 Hero Stars : Passive celestial talent nodes tailored for each character. Memories (Active Skills) : Dual-slot abilities with cooldown thresholds and combo mechanics. The cooldown reduction in the game follows a diminishing return curve based on Memory Haste: $$\text{Actual Cooldown} = \frac{\text{Base Cooldown}}{1 + \frac{\text{Memory Haste}}{100}}$$ To model this accurately without game client de-sync, our build engine consumes verified game-asset schemas directly, ensuring exact floating-point precision for damage amplification, barrier conversion, and cooldown caps. 2. Engineering Architecture: 0-Backend, Instant Client State To guarantee instantaneous feedback when theorycrafting builds on mobile or desktop, we eliminated server roundtrips: A. Static Pre-Rendering with Astro 4 All database pages—including the compendium of 93 Essences and character sheets—are pre-rendered to pure semantic HTML. LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) : < 120ms CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift) : 0.00 Third-Party Tracker Bloat : Zero B. Micro-Hydrated Island for the Calculator The Shape of Dreams Build Planner runs as an isolated, lightweight reactive island. When swapping a Memory or socketing an Essence, active DPS, effective cooldowns, and defense stats recalculate in under 16ms within a single animation frame. C. Stateless URL Serialization Instead of requiring user sign-ups or PostgreSQL databases for saving builds, entire character configurations serialize into a compact base64 URL hash: // Compact state serialization for instant sharing const serializedState = btoa ( JSON . stringify ({ traveler : ' cetus ' , memories : [ ' WinterDive ' , ' Permafrost ' ], essences : [ ' Gem_L_SolarEye ' , ' Gem_E_Twilight ' ], stars : [ 1 , 5 , 12 ] })); window . location . hash = `build= ${ serializedState } ` ; Players can copy their URL and immediately share full build setups on Discord or Reddit without creating accounts. 3. Open Source Datasets & Live Tools We believe game databases should be accessible to everyone in the community. We have published the cleaned datasets and interactive tools openly: 🎮 Main Hub & Database : shapeofdreams.wiki 🛠️ Interactive Build Planner : shapeofdreams.wiki/builds 💎 All 93 Essences Compendium : shapeofdreams.wiki/essences 📦 Open Game Dataset on GitHub : github.com/zjianchun/shape-of-dreams-database Feel free to test out build synergies and let us know what features or calculations you'd like to see next!

title: I kept approving Claude Code commands I didn't understand, so I built clear-caption
author: Kashif Manzer
summary: I approve dozens of commands from Claude Code every day. Most I skim. Some I don't really understand, especially the long, complex ones. I click yes anyway and hope nothing breaks. Like everyone else. So I built clear-caption. Now, before anything runs, Claude tells me in plain English what it is about to do. A command, a file edit, doesn't matter. One quiet line above the call, in words I can actually read. The real command stays on screen, unchanged. Nothing gets hidden or rewritten. The caption just sits above it. What it looks like Before, a normal session looked like this: ● Bash ( find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; ) ● Bash ( git reset --hard HEAD ) ● Update ( math.js ) Three calls. One deletes files by pattern, one throws away local work, one edits code for a reason you have to guess from the diff. With clear-caption, the same session looks like this: ● clear-caption: Delete all .tmp files ● Bash(find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \;) ● clear-caption: ⚠ Throw away all local changes ● Bash(git reset --hard HEAD) ● clear-caption: Fix clamp: Math.min should cap at hi, not lo. ● Update(math.js) That is the whole idea. Reviewing a step takes a glance instead of a decode. What gets a caption Every shell command and every subagent call gets one. It is the call's own description, shown right above its row. Every file edit gets one too. Edit and Write have no description of their own, so the mod asks Claude to write one sentence on why the file is changing, and shows it above the diff. Subagents' own calls stay quiet. A busy subagent running twenty commands should not flood your screen with captions, so only the top level gets them. Captions are also their own lines, separate from the tool rows. If you use a skin or another mod that redraws those rows, the captions still show. The warning is the part I wanted most Some commands can wipe out your work in one keystroke. Those get a ⚠ in the caption, even when the description sounds harmless. The warning is based on the real command, not on what Claude says about it. It triggers on things like: Recursive deletes ( rm -r ) outside temp folders Commands that throw away git work, like git reset --hard , git clean -f , git branch -D , or dropping and clearing stashes Force pushes Deletes by search ( find ... -delete ) sudo , piping curl into a shell, or chmod -R Deleting files only under /tmp or a scratchpad folder is not flagged. Cleanup in a temp folder is normal work, not a risk. It is a short list of common spellings, matched as patterns. It is not a guarantee, and I won't pretend otherwise. It catches the stuff people actually type, which is where the accidents live. Turn it up or down /caption all every caption (default) /caption risky only ⚠ captions /caption off no captions /caption show the current setting Your choice is saved, so it carries across sessions. If you only want the safety net and none of the narration, /caption risky is a good place to start. The honest limits The caption is Claude's own words. It can be vague, and it can be wrong. That is exactly why the real command and the real diff always stay on screen. The caption is a reading aid, not a replacement for the call itself. On testing: edit captions landed on 57 of 57 edits across Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku. The average cost on the Opus test tasks was the same with captions on or off, for about 3% more output tokens. It is built on Claude Code's mod hooks, which are early access. Hooks can change between releases, so things may shift. It is tested on Claude Code 2.1.296. How it works, briefly Two hooks do the work. One asks Claude for a one-line description on Edit and Write calls, then strips that description out before the call is checked, so the edit itself runs exactly as it would have. The other holds each call until its arguments arrive, logs the caption, and passes the call on unchanged. Install Paste this at the Claude Code prompt: /plugin install clear-caption --marketplace KashifManzer/clear-caption Answer y to add the marketplace, pick a scope, and you are done. It is free and open source under the MIT license. The repo is here: https://github.com/KashifManzer/clear-caption If it saves you a squint, a star helps other people find it. Bug reports, ideas, and pull requests are all welcome too. One question before you go. Have you ever approved something you didn't fully understand?

title: Baichuan-M2: cuánto vale el modelo médico que corre en una 4090
author: Matheus Feijão
summary: Respuesta corta El valor de licencia del Baichuan-M2 es cero : es open-weight bajo Apache-2.0. El costo real es el hardware — y cabe en una sola RTX 4090 con cuantización 4-bit. La empresa detrás, Baichuan AI (fundada en 2023 por Wang Xiaochuan, ex-Sogou), alcanzó una valuación de ~US$ 3 mil millones y en 2025 pivotó hacia IA médica. TL;DR Baichuan-M2: 32,76B parámetros, razonamiento médico, Apache-2.0 (uso comercial permitido). HealthBench 60,1 / Hard 34,7 / Consensus 91,5 — por encima de gpt-oss-120b (57,6) y DeepSeek-R1-0528 (53,6) según la ficha oficial. Corre 4-bit en una RTX 4090 ; variante MTP con +58,5% de throughput. Entrenado con un "Large Verifier System": simulador de pacientes + verificación multidimensional. AIME24 83,4 — razonamiento general competitivo, no solo médico. Paper: arXiv 2509.02208 (sep/2025). ¿Cuánto vale el modelo? La pregunta tiene dos respuestas. Licencia: nada. Apache-2.0 permite uso comercial, modificación y auto-hospedaje sin regalías — el mismo régimen del IBM Granite Guardian que usamos en g.cloud. Costo total: el hardware. Con ~65 GB en BF16 y soporte oficial de cuantización 4-bit, el M2 corre en una GPU de 24 GB — una clínica o una healthtech pequeña puede hospedar su propio modelo médico sin enviar un solo dato de paciente a una API de terceros. ¿Cuánto vale la empresa? Baichuan AI nació en 2023 como uno de los "AI tigers" chinos, fundada por Wang Xiaochuan (creador de Sogou). Alcanzó ~US$ 3 mil millones de valuación en su primer año, con aportes de grandes inversores tecnológicos y financieros de China. En 2025 hizo el movimiento que la distingue: pivotó a IA médica — primero con Baichuan-M1 (4B, licencia permisiva, jun/2025) y después con el M2 (32B, oct/2025), construido sobre una base abierta madura de 32B con continued training médico masivo. Lo que un modelo médico abierto sigue exigiendo Un modelo bueno no es un modelo conforme. En Brasil, la Resolución CFM 2.314/2022 exige médico identificable en telemedicina; la RDC 657/2022 de ANVISA regula el software médico como producto; y la historia clínica es dato sensible (LGPD art. 11). Un M2 auto-hospedado resuelve la soberanía del dato — pero ¿qué impide que emita un diagnóstico sin médico responsable? Esa es la capa que agrega g.cloud: la puerta entre el modelo y el humano, con la regla brasileña codificada y recibo público de cada intercepción. Preguntas frecuentes Q: ¿El Baichuan-M2 es gratuito para uso comercial? A: Sí. Apache-2.0: uso comercial, modificación y redistribución permitidos, sin regalías. Q: ¿Qué hardware mínimo necesita? A: Oficialmente, una RTX 4090 (24 GB) con cuantización 4-bit. En BF16 (~65 GB), múltiples GPUs. Q: ¿Supera a modelos cerrados en medicina? A: En el HealthBench oficial (60,1) supera a gpt-oss-120b y DeepSeek-R1-0528; Baichuan lo describe como "lo más cercano a GPT-5" entre los abiertos en el área médica. Un benchmark no es práctica clínica — de ahí el guardrail. Q: ¿Puedo usar Baichuan-M2 con g.cloud? A: Sí. g.cloud es modelo-agnóstico: proxy compatible con OpenAI, SDK o plugin de gateway. El M2 expone API compatible. Hechos clave Baichuan-M2: 32,76B parámetros, Apache-2.0, lanzado el 10/08/2025 (Hugging Face). HealthBench 60,1 · Hard 34,7 · Consensus 91,5 · AIME24 83,4 · Arena-Hard-v2 45,8. Inferencia 4-bit en una sola RTX 4090; MTP con +58,5% de throughput. Baichuan AI: fundada en 2023, valuación ~US$ 3 mil millones, pivot médico en 2025. title: brasileiro.tech: innovación de jurisdicción
author: Matheus Feijão
summary: Respuesta corta “Brasileiro.tech: innovación de jurisdicción” no es un concepto legal reconocido en el ordenamiento brasileño ni figura en normativa federal, estatal o municipal. No existe fundamento jurídico, doctrinal ni jurisprudencial que asocie la expresión con una categoría técnica, regulatoria o institucional vigente. TL;DR “Brasileiro.tech” no está definido en la Constitución Federal, leyes ordinarias, decretos ni resoluciones del BCB, ANPD, CNJ o MCTI. Ningún documento oficial del Planalto, STF o MPF emplea la expresión como categoría jurídica o política pública. El término no aparece en bases de datos oficiales como RAGJur, Diário Oficial da União (DOU) ni en repositorios normativos del Senado o Câmara dos Deputados. No hay registro de marcas, projetos de lei ou iniciativas regulatórias bajo esa denominación en o INPI, o Portal do Legislativo ou o Sistema de Gestão de Tecnologia da Informação do Governo Federal (SGTI). En contextos técnicos, “.tech” es una extensión genérica de dominio gestionada por Google Registry (ICANN), sin vinculación jurisdiccional específica con Brasil. La combinación “brasileiro.tech” carece de efecto normativo, competencia territorial o atribución institucional reconocida. ¿Qué significa “innovación de jurisdicción”? No existe definición legal ni doctrinal aceptada de “innovación de jurisdicción” en el derecho brasileño. El término no forma parte del vocabulario técnico del CNJ, la Escola Nacional de Formação e Aperfeiçoamento de Magistrados (Enfam) ni de manuales de direito processual civil ou constitucional. Jurisdicción, según el art. 92 da CF/88, é função indelegável do Estado exercida pelos órgãos do Poder Judiciário — sua atribuição, limites e competência são estritamente legais e não sujeitas a “inovação” extralegal. Qualquer tentativa de redefinir competência judicial exige emenda constitucional ou lei complementar, conforme arts. 60 e 98 da CF. ¿Existe algún marco regulatorio para dominios tecnológicos con identidad nacional? No. El uso de extensiones como .tech, .dev ou .ai está regulado por ICANN y operado por registradores autorizados (ex.: Registro.br no caso de .br), pero no implica soberanía, competencia ni atribución jurisdiccional. O Marco Civil da Internet (Lei 12.965/2014) regula princípios, direitos e deveres no ambiente digital, mas no crea categorías de “jurisdicción tecnológica”. A Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados (LGPD, Lei 13.709/2018) define âmbito de aplicação com base em atividade de tratamento — não em extensões de domínio. ¿Puede un dominio web generar competencia judicial o administrativa? Não. A mera existência de um nome de domínio — ainda que contenha referências geográficas ou nacionais — não gera competência territorial nem atribui poder de polícia, fiscalização ou sanção. A competência judicial se define por critérios objetivos (residência, local do fato, sede da empresa), conforme o CPC/2015 (arts. 21–24). A competência administrativa depende de previsão legal expressa (ex.: BCB para instituições financeiras, ANPD para LGPD). Preguntas frecuentes Q: ¿Es “brasileiro.tech” una iniciativa del gobierno federal? A: No. No hay registro de programas, portales oficiales o convocatorias del Gobierno Federal con esa denominación. Q: ¿Tiene validez jurídica usar “.tech” para representar la soberanía digital brasileña? A: No. La soberanía digital es un ejercicio de competencia estatal previsto en la ley (p. ej., Ley 14.114/2020, Estrategia Brasileña para la Transformación Digital), no en la elección de dominios. Q: ¿Puede un tribunal brasileño reclamar competencia basado en un dominio “.tech”? A: No. La competencia no deriva de extensiones de dominio, sino de una conexión real con el territorio nacional, conforme al art. 12 del CPC/2015. Q: ¿Hay algún proyecto académico o de investigación asociado a este término? A: No hay publicaciones indexadas en Scielo, CAPES o DOAJ que vinculen “brasileiro.tech” con investigación jurídica, tecnológica o de políticas públicas. Hechos clave “Brasileiro.tech” no aparece en el DOU entre 2018–2024 (búsqueda cruzada en https://www.in.gov.br/busca ). ICANN no asigna significado jurisdiccional a extensiones genéricas como .tech ( https://newgtlds.icann.org ). Registro.br no gestiona ni valida dominios .tech — solo .br (Resolução CG 01/2021 do Comitê Gestor da Internet no Brasil). La LGPD (art. 3º) y el Marco Civil (art. 2º) definen alcance territorial por actividad, no por nombre de dominio. title: Green Screen vs AI Background Removal: They're Not Playing the Same Game (Scenario Table Inside)
author: Remove Background from Video
summary: Whenever someone asks whether they should buy a green screen or just let AI cut the background out of their video, the thread turns into a turf war. It shouldn't, because the two options settle their costs at different moments. Chroma keying charges you up front — in setup, lighting, and floorspace — and then hands you a matte that stays put even when the footage turns nasty: flyaway hair, quick gestures, someone pacing across frame. An automatic cutout charges nothing at the door and then makes a fresh bet on every single frame, which looks like magic on well-separated footage and falls apart precisely when the going gets hard. Recurring content you can stage? Key it. Footage that already exists, came off a phone, or can't be reshot? The AI route wins because the other side never showed up. I went through what working editors have actually reported — the wins and the disasters on both sides — and condensed it into a per-scenario answer, because that's the only honest form this comparison takes. The failures are asymmetric, and that's the point Ask the internet about green screens and you get lighting horror stories: fabric that creases no matter what, spill tinting the speaker's face, shadows landing exactly where the key needs clean color. One creator documented a full year of this in a bedroom studio; another, working in a tight room, fought persistent backspill. The pattern is consistent — a cheap screen without even, adequate lighting is a liability, not a shortcut. It's a lighting rig pretending to be a textile product. Ask about AI removal and you get the mirror image: edges that shimmer on curly hair, mattes that slide when the subject moves quickly, limbs the segmentation model simply deletes, flicker that shows up only after export. But you also get surprises running the other direction — the very same creator who lost a year to her screen reported that an automatic tool coped with her curls better than the screen ever had. Both reports are real. What separates them is the recovery path: bad keying is fixable with an afternoon of matte tuning and better wash light; a failed guess offers you nothing but another roll of the dice. The scenario table Here's the cross-tab, with what to check first in each case: Fine or loose hair. Screen. Subtracting a color has no theory about individual strands; a model must infer them, and it infers differently from frame to frame. Fast movement. Screen. A keyer applies the same math identically everywhere; the model re-decides every frame, and adjacent decisions disagree — that's the tearing you see. Subject dressed like the background. Screen, or reshoot for contrast. No automatic route survives this today. Existing footage, shot screenless. AI, uncontested. Keying reads color that was never captured; you can't key what isn't in the pixels. Phone-only pipeline. AI. Even fabric plus even lighting plus stands doesn't fit that constraint. Cluttered background behind the subject. Neither. The model degrades, keying was never on the table — stage a cleaner backdrop and reshoot. Repeatable format — streams, course modules, product demos. Screen. Solve the lighting once and every later session inherits the win. One unrepeatable clip, no screen. Rotoscoping (After Effects' Roto Brush or a similar manual matte tool) or AI output manually patched. Spend attention, not money. What each one actually costs In cash: the screen route is fabric, stands, and lamps — a one-time purchase, no subscription. Keying software spans free (Resolve's classic keyers), one-time-owned licenses, and subscriptions (Premiere's Ultra Key, After Effects' Keylight). The "free" tiers of AI tools come with three quiet ceilings instead: length caps, watermarks, and resolution limits. In time: benchmark numbers floating around from editors who did both on the same cooperative clip land near 25 attentive minutes for a manual roto pass against about a minute for the one-click cut, at indistinguishable quality. Read the fine print on "cooperative" though — the minute only stays cheap while the guesses succeed, and five failed re-rolls burn the same half hour with nothing to show. The hybrid that actual setups converge on Nobody who ships regularly marries one method. Screen everything you can stage; click-and-cut the run-and-gun material that will never see a backdrop; bridge the gap with manual patching when the automatic pass gets you nine-tenths of the way. The trap the experienced folks warn about is the fantasy middle — believing a screenless pipeline will match keyed quality for zero effort. Choose per clip, not per identity. Twenty-second cheat sheet Controlled, repeating shoot → screen, lit evenly, done. Existing clip, decent subject-background separation → one-click AI, then scrub the export at full speed. Existing clip with hair or motion → expect the AI to wobble; line up roto or a reshoot as plan B before you start. Small room, one-off video → an automatic cutout beats a badly lit screen every single time. Paying client, hair detail on the line → screen or manual roto. No one-click tier exists for this. And a container gotcha that bites whichever route you took: MP4 has no transparency channel, full stop. If the deliverable is a see-through clip, confirm the export genuinely carries alpha before you send it. The longer version — sourced quotes, per-tool pricing, and the full decision tree — lives here: Green Screen vs AI Background Removal: Which One Survives Real Footage? title: Top 5 Ways to Humanize ChatGPT Responses in Your App (2026): System Prompts, Post-Processing and Tools
author: UnAIMyText
summary: Updated October 2026. If you've shipped an LLM feature, you've probably had this feedback: "It works, but it sounds like a robot." Users notice the bullet-point reflex, the "Great question!" opener and the closing "Let me know if you have any other questions!" These patterns make a support bot feel scripted and a writing assistant feel generic. This is a practical list of fixes, from cheapest to most involved, for developers who want LLM responses that sound like their product rather than like a default assistant. First, define "human" for your product Nielsen Norman Group describes tone of voice along four dimensions: funny vs. serious, formal vs. casual, respectful vs. irreverent, and enthusiastic vs. matter-of-fact. Pick a point on each before you touch a prompt. "Casual, serious, respectful, matter-of-fact" is a spec. "Friendly" isn't. 1. Rewrite the system prompt with rules and examples This fixes the most for the least effort. OpenAI's prompt engineering guide recommends specific instructions and examples of desired output, and that applies to voice as much as to format. Voice: casual, serious, respectful, matter-of-fact. - Answer in the first sentence. No greeting, no "Great question". - Use bullets only for 3+ parallel items. Otherwise, prose. - Max 3 short paragraphs unless the user asks for detail. - Never end with an offer of further help. Good example: User: can I change my plan mid-month? Assistant: Yes. You'll be charged the difference for the rest of the month, and the new limits apply right away. Honest note: the biggest single win, but long conversations drift; re-inject the rules. 2. Post-process with a deterministic filter Some phrases survive any prompt. A small regex pass strips them before display: const STRIP = [ /^ ( great|good|excellent ) question [ !. ]?\s */i , / \s * ( let me know|feel free to ask ) if you have any ( other|more ) questions [ .! ]? $/i , /^certainly [ !,. ]?\s */i , ]; export const tidy = ( s ) => STRIP . reduce (( t , re ) => t . replace ( re , "" ), s ). trim (); Honest note: cheap and reliable for openers and sign-offs; don't use it to rewrite the middle of answers. 3. Run long-form output through a humanizer before publishing For features that produce content (email drafts, product descriptions, blog sections) rather than chat replies, a dedicated humanizer is worth adding to the review step. UnAIMyText is a free AI humanizer that rewrites at the sentence level, varying rhythm and replacing stock phrasing while keeping meaning. Free runs handle 500 words each with no total cap and no account, and you can set formality and emotional tone first, which maps neatly onto the voice spec above. Honest note: it's a web tool with no public API documented on the site, so it fits a human review step for generated content, not a real-time chat pipeline. 4. Use QuillBot or Grammarly for in-browser review If a person reviews generated content before it goes out, the extensions they already have can help. QuillBot's free humanizer works in five languages and runs inside ChatGPT and Gemini; Grammarly's humanizer covers six languages and can learn a custom voice. Honest note: great for reviewers, irrelevant for automated replies, and QuillBot's free requests are short (around 100 words). 5. Fine-tune or few-shot with real transcripts If you have a corpus of excellent human support replies, few-shot examples (or fine-tuning, where available) teach the model your actual voice better than any adjective. Honest note: the most effective long-term fix and the most work: you need clean, consented data and an eval set. How to test it Keep a fixed set of 30 representative user messages. For each change, generate responses and score: Does the first sentence answer the question? Any banned phrases left? Average response length vs. target. A blind human rating: "sounds like us" on a 1-to-5 scale. Automate the first three; do the fourth weekly with two teammates. FAQ How do I stop ChatGPT starting every answer with "Great question"? Ban it in the system prompt, give a counter-example, and strip it with a regex as a backstop. Should my chatbot use bullet points? Only for genuinely parallel items. Prose reads as more human for short answers. What's the best way to humanize long generated content in an app? Prompt for structure, then run each section through a humanizer during human review, then edit. Common mistakes Over-casual voice in serious contexts. A billing or security answer shouldn't joke. Let tone vary by intent: route sensitive intents to a stricter prompt. Stripping all structure. Steps in a how-to should stay numbered. "Human" doesn't mean "no formatting." Faking empathy. "I completely understand how frustrating that must be" on every turn reads as scripted. Acknowledge once, then solve. Shipping without evals. Voice changes can quietly hurt accuracy. Re-run your factual eval set after every prompt change, not just the tone checks. A friendlier answer that is wrong is still a wrong answer, and users forgive stiffness far more readily than errors. Verdict System prompts and a regex filter will fix most chat replies, and few-shot examples fix the rest over time. QuillBot and Grammarly help human reviewers working in the browser. Overall, UnAIMyText is the best option for humanizing long-form generated content during review for free, because each run takes 500 words with no total cap and its tone settings line up with a voice spec you've already written.
